podcast.title: Bunk Swap with Cliff Burton (September 27, 1986)
podcast.body: On the night of the fatal bus crash that killed Cliff Burton, Kirk Hammett's usual bunk was chosen by Burton after a card game. Hammett, indifferent, opted for another bunk, inadvertently avoiding the fatal spot. "Cliff drew the Ace of Spades which was the high card so he got to choose his bunk first. And he chose the bunk that Kirk Hammett had been using."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Stupid History 2

podcast.title: "It's Alive" Exhibition at ROM
podcast.body: Hammett's extensive, comprehensive, and well-preserved collection of classic horror movie posters and artwork is deemed significant enough to be featured in major museum exhibitions, including "It's Alive: Classic Horror and Sci-Fi Art from the Kirk Hammett Collection" at the Royal Ontario Museum (ROM) in Toronto. This exhibition ran from July 12, 2019, until January 5, 2020, with plans to tour other museums globally thereafter. "This collection is so big and so comprehensive and so well preserved that it's the subject of exhibitions at major museums, including the Royal Ontario Museum in Toronto."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Kirk Hammett’s Movie Poster Collection ｜ Bonus Podcast

podcast.title: Childhood Interest in Horror
podcast.body: Hammett's fascination with horror began around age five or six, in the late 1960s or early 1970s. He was initially drawn to the genre because it offered a distinctly different feel and atmosphere compared to the prevalent Disney movies and cartoons that defined much of the culture he experienced as a child. "It was something that I was attracted to initially because it was so different and had a different sort of feel and atmosphere to a lot of the culture I was getting at the time as a 5 or 6 year old, you know, that would have entailed a lot of Disney movies and cartoons."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Kirk Hammett’s Movie Poster Collection ｜ Bonus Podcast

podcast.title: Collection Focus on Universal Monsters
podcast.body: While he enjoys most horror movies from the turn of the last century to modern times, Hammett primarily focuses his collection on classic Universal horror monsters and movies from the early 1930s. His key interest lies in characters such as Frankenstein, Dracula, The Mummy, Wolfman, Phantom of the Opera, Creature from the Black Lagoon, and The Hunchback. "But I try to keep it to what I really love and what means the most to me, which is the classic universal horror monsters and those movies that came out in the early 30s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Kirk Hammett’s Movie Poster Collection ｜ Bonus Podcast

podcast.title: Discovery of Rare Posters
podcast.body: When Hammett started collecting over three decades ago, the existence of a "Frankenstein 3 sheet" or a "Mummy 3 sheet" poster was entirely unknown. He subsequently found both, and these pieces currently represent the only known copies of their kind in the world. "when I first started 30 years ago, no one knew that there was a Frankenstein three sheet out there or a mummy three sheet. I mean, I found both."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Kirk Hammett’s Movie Poster Collection ｜ Bonus Podcast

podcast.title: Diverse Horror Memorabilia
podcast.body: Beyond movie posters, Hammett's collection encompasses a wide array of horror memorabilia, including props (items used in movies), toys (both vintage and continuously produced modern ones), masks, artwork, paintings, comics, original art, and sculptures. He differentiates his collecting from genres like Star Wars or Star Trek, strictly adhering to horror. "I, I tried to keep it to a horror movie posters, props, which are, you know, items that were used in certain movies. I love, I love the toys."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Kirk Hammett’s Movie Poster Collection ｜ Bonus Podcast

podcast.title: Early Entry into Collecting
podcast.body: Hammett began collecting movie posters over 30 years ago, when the hobby was still underground and had relatively few participants. This allowed him to acquire available pieces at "sensible" prices because there was less competition among collectors. "I got into this hobby when it was so underground, over 30 years ago, there weren't a lot of movie poster collectors."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Kirk Hammett’s Movie Poster Collection ｜ Bonus Podcast

podcast.title: Exhibition Content
podcast.body: The "It's Alive" exhibition at the Royal Ontario Museum features his "core collection," specifically "my hundred best pieces," which totals over a hundred items. This selection broadly represents the horror genre from the turn of the last century to modern times, designed to illustrate the evolution of horror movie posters and the cultural trends reflected in them. "The collection that, of things that are going to, to the Toronto Museum is my core collection or in other words, my hundred best pieces."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Kirk Hammett’s Movie Poster Collection ｜ Bonus Podcast

podcast.title: Exhibition Goals
podcast.body: Hammett hopes that visitors to his exhibition will first and foremost recognize the beauty and grandeur of the collected works and be "blown away" by seeing such a concentration of great pieces together. Beyond aesthetic appreciation, he aims for the exhibition to educate the public about the art of movie posters, their historical contribution to culture, and their evolution from the turn of the last century to the present day. "Well, first and foremost, I hope that people will see these things and just get, we'll recognize the beauty of it and the grand tour of it and just get blown away by seeing all this stuff in one spot because when you have all these really great pieces and they're all together, you get the synergy going and it's for me, it's a really cool energy and it feels really good and it's overwhelmingly just cool just to be surround by cool horror pieces if you're a fan."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Kirk Hammett’s Movie Poster Collection ｜ Bonus Podcast

podcast.title: Favorite Piece: The Mummy 3 Sheet
podcast.body: Hammett's absolute favorite piece in his collection, irrespective of its monetary value, is "The Mummy 3 sheet" poster, an image so significant to him that it is also depicted on his guitar. He finds himself completely engrossed by its colors, composition, and overall richness, describing it as having an "amazing effect" that allows his mind to dive in totally and get lost. "You know, it probably would be the Mummy 3 sheet. I love that image. It's on my guitar. You know, when I look at it, I just get lost in the colors of it, the composition, just the luscious of it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Kirk Hammett’s Movie Poster Collection ｜ Bonus Podcast

podcast.title: First Horror Movie Experience
podcast.body: His first horror movie experience was watching "Day of the Triffids," likely from the late 1950s or early 1960s. This viewing made a strong impression on him, prompting him to actively seek out more horror-related stories across various media such as comic books, magazines, and books. "Yes, a movie called Day of the Triffids."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Kirk Hammett’s Movie Poster Collection ｜ Bonus Podcast

podcast.title: Holy Grail Items
podcast.body: Hammett's "holy grail" items, pieces he would love to find but which have not yet been discovered, include a "Bride of Frankenstein 3 sheet" and a "Dracula 3 sheet." These are billboard-sized posters from the 1920s that, if found, would be incredible additions to his collection. "Well, there's a lot of pieces out there that I would love to have that have not just been found at all, you know, like a bright of Frankenstein, three sheet, you know, Dracula, three sheet."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Kirk Hammett’s Movie Poster Collection ｜ Bonus Podcast

podcast.title: Horror Movie and Memorabilia Passion
podcast.body: Kirk Hammett has maintained a lifelong passion for horror movies and horror memorabilia, with his primary obsession being posters from old sci-fi and horror films. This interest began in his childhood, around the age of five or six. "Kirk has always been a fan of horror movies. And Kirk is a fan of horror memorabilia. But his biggest passion are posters from old sci-fi and horror movies."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Kirk Hammett’s Movie Poster Collection ｜ Bonus Podcast

podcast.title: John Marshall as Guitar Tech
podcast.body: Kirk Hammett of Metallica has John Marshall as his dedicated guitar tech. Marshall, who previously played guitar for Metal Church, transitioned to this role for Metallica. "John Marshall was a guitarist for the band Metal Church before he was picked to be Kirk Hammett's guitar tech in Metallica."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: We Are The Road Crew - A History of Roadies

podcast.title: Preference for Thematic Horror
podcast.body: Hammett prefers horror movies with supernatural, monster, outer space, or paranormal themes, tending to avoid overtly violent horror. He sees "torture porn" as a "cheap thrill" that often lacks the plot and intrigue he values, making it difficult for him to recognize any artistry in it. "I tend to shy away from horror movies that are overtly violent. You know, I like horror but I don't like horror for the sake of it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

Cliff drew the Ace of Spades, giving him first choice, and he chose the bunk Kirk Hammett had been using, making the incident a tragic twist of fate. "Cliff drew the Ace of Spades which was the high card so he got to choose his bunk first."

xref.title: Cliff Burton's Death (1986)
xref.body: Former Metallica bassist Cliff Burton died in a tour bus accident in 1986. His initials (CBL) and a transcription of his song "Orion" are tattooed on James Hetfield as a tribute. "That's a transcription of the song Orion, which is in tribute to former Metallica bass player Cliff Burton, who died in a tour bus accident in 1986."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rock'n'Roll Tattoos

xref.title: Fatal Tour Bus Accident (September 27, 1986)
xref.body: Cliff Burton died on September 27, 1986, in Sweden during Metallica's tour for "Master of Puppets." After drawing the Ace of Spades to choose his bunk on the bus, he slept in Kirk Hammett's usual spot. The bus hit black ice around 7 a.m., causing the driver to lose control, resulting in the bus leaving the road and rolling onto its side. "He was the one who was killed and then awful tour bus accident in Sweden back on September 27, 1986."

xref.title: Extensive Horror Movie Memorabilia Collection
xref.body: Kirk Hammett has an absolute obsession with old horror movie posters and memorabilia, amassing one of the most comprehensive collections in the world. His interest in horror movies began at the age of five or six, drawn by their distinct feel and atmosphere compared to the Disney movies and cartoons prevalent in the late 1960s and early 1970s. He describes feeling an immediate attraction to the different type of story horror presented, pursuing it through comic books, magazines, movies, and books. His first horror movie was "Day of the Triffids," likely from the late 1950s or early 1960s. His collection is so exceptional that it tours museums globally. "His collection is one of the most comprehensive in the world."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Hobbies of Musicians

xref.title: Founding Member's Firing
xref.body: On April 11, 1983, while in New York to record their debut album, Metallica fired co-founder Dave Mustaine at 9 AM while he was sleeping. The band had already hired Kirk Hammett as his replacement, with no warning or second chance given. Mustaine was sent back to California on a four-day Greyhound bus ride. "On April 11, 1983, Metallica was in New York to record their debut while in the middle of the night. It was the day that Mustaine was fired."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
